result.topic: Lane B1: structured-reasoning methods (ToT, GoT, FoT, self-consistency, LATS, Reflexion, debate) and search-based coding agents, and whether they bear on B01 (fix rounds creating new defects), B04 and B13

claims.claim: Tree of Thoughts (Yao 2023) gains were measured only on toy puzzle tasks with an older non-reasoning model.
claims.what_sources_say: The abstract names Game of 24, Creative Writing and Mini Crosswords. On Game of 24, GPT-4 with chain-of-thought solved 4% and ToT 74%. The abstract gives no cost or call multiplier. A secondary comparison page (not a measurement) puts ToT at roughly 5-20x the compute of plain CoT. These are puzzles with explicit search structure, not software engineering, and the model predates 2025-2026 reasoning models.

sources.title: Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
Search results on ToT vs CoT compute (secondary blogs)

claims.claim: Graph of Thoughts (Besta 2023) improves on ToT through aggregation and refinement of thoughts, at lower cost.
claims.what_sources_say: Abstract: thoughts are vertices in a graph that can be combined (aggregated), distilled or refined by feedback loops. It reports sorting quality up 62% over ToT and cost down over 31%. Only sorting is named, no model is named on the page, and the cost is relative to ToT, not to a plain single prompt or to CoT. Sorting is a toy task. I did not read the full paper.

sources.title: Graph of Thoughts: Solving Elaborate Problems with Large Language Models

claims.claim: Forest-of-Thought (Bi 2024) shows significant gains from multiple reasoning trees with sparse activation, self-correction and consensus.
claims.what_sources_say: Only the abstract was read. It says FoT integrates several reasoning trees with sparse activation, dynamic self-correction and consensus-guided decision-making, and claims 'significantly enhances' reasoning. No benchmark, model, number or cost appears on the page, and I did not read the full paper. Treat as an unverified assertion; it targets logical and math reasoning, not code.

sources.title: Forest-of-Thought: Scaling Test-Time Compute for Enhancing LLM Reasoning

claims.claim: Complex reasoning strategies (debate, Reflexion, ToT-style) mostly win because they get more compute; at matched compute plain self-consistency often matches or beats them.
claims.what_sources_say: Reasoning in Token Economies (abstract, fetched): with comparable compute, CoT self-consistency 'frequently outperforms' strategies from the literature, and multi-agent debate and Reflexion can get worse as budget grows. Per a search snippet of Huang et al. 2023, on GSM8K debate underperforms majority voting at equal response count. A counterpoint snippet (an ACL 2026 student paper) reports debate and mixture-of-agents beating self-consistency by 1.3 and 2.7 points on MMLU-Pro at equal compute, so the effect is small and benchmark-dependent. Models and numbers for the first paper were not on the abstract page. All are math or QA benchmarks, not coding.

sources.title: Reasoning in Token Economies: Budget-Aware Evaluation of LLM Reasoning Strategies
Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
Multi-Agent Reasoning Improves Compute Efficiency: Pareto-Optimal Test-Time Scaling

claims.claim: The ToT-style gains persist with 2025-2026 reasoning models that search internally.
claims.what_sources_say: Two searches found no controlled study that re-tests ToT prompting on o1/o3/R1-class models at equal budget, and no study showing it hurts. Sources that say reasoning models make ToT unnecessary are blogs and tutorials (interpretation, not measurement). Indirect evidence: Rethinking Thinking Tokens (abstract fetched) reports that iterative pipelines (Parallel-Distill-Refine) beat single-pass long-CoT at matched sequential budget, +11% on AIME 2024 and +9% on AIME 2025 with lower latency (models not named on the page, absolute or relative unstated), so parallel-draft-then-distill does help on verifiable math even with current models. A budget-guided MCTS paper (abstract only) reports beating budget-agnostic tree search, which is a comparison among search variants, not against long CoT. So the honest position is: untested for ToT proper, some evidence for parallel-then-distill on math with verifiers.

sources.title: Rethinking Thinking Tokens: LLMs as Improvement Operators
Aligning Tree-Search Policies with Fixed Token Budgets in Test-Time Scaling of LLMs
Web search: ToT on reasoning models (blogs/tutorials only)

claims.claim: Agentless's multi-candidate sampling with test-based reranking improves SWE-bench Lite over single-patch generation.
claims.what_sources_say: Measured (full paper, SWE-bench Lite, 300 issues, ablation Table 4): majority voting alone 77 resolved (25.67%); plus regression-test filter 81 (27.00%); plus a model-generated reproduction-test filter 96 (32.00%). 40 patches per issue (4 localization sets x 10 patches). Average cost $0.70 and about 78k tokens per issue overall. The reproduction test gave most of the gain, but of 300 issues only 94 reproduction tests printed 'resolved' under the true patch, so the verifier is noisy. Oracle ceiling over the candidates is 126 (42.0%), so selection recovers 96 of 126. Performance plateaued near 40 samples. Model and date predate current frontier models (2024); I did not read the last 24k characters of the page.

sources.title: Agentless: Demystifying LLM-based Software Engineering Agents (HTML)

claims.claim: MCTS or tree-search coding agents (SWE-Search, CodeTree) beat linear agents on SWE-bench.
claims.what_sources_say: SWE-Search (abstract): MCTS plus a Value Agent and a Discriminator Agent that debates; value function is LLM-based (numeric and qualitative), not test-based; reports a 23% relative improvement across five models on SWE-bench, with models, absolute scores and cost not on the page. CodeTree (abstract): unified tree of strategy, solution and refinement stages, guided by execution feedback plus LLM-agent feedback; GPT-4o gets 95.1 HumanEval, 98.7 MBPP, 43.0 CodeContests; SWE-bench gain stated only as 'significant', no number or cost. Both are authors' self-reports, mostly on function-level benchmarks (HumanEval/MBPP are near saturated) or relative gains. No equal-cost comparison against simple best-of-n was in either abstract.

sources.title: SWE-Search: Enhancing Software Agents with Monte Carlo Tree Search and Iterative Refinement
CodeTree: Agent-guided Tree Search for Code Generation

claims.claim: Sampling many candidate patches and selecting with executed or generated tests works on SWE-bench at large cost, and the selection step is the weak link.
claims.what_sources_say: CodeMonkeys (abstract fetched): voting over model-written tests plus a final selection trajectory resolved 57.4% of SWE-bench Verified for about $2,300 total; selecting among existing top submissions reached 66.2%, above the best single member (the model and oracle-gap figures were not on the page). SWE-agent appendix (snippet only): pass@6 32.7% vs about 17.9% single-run on Lite, so the gap between 'some candidate is right' and 'we pick it' is large. Trae's blog (vendor, snippet only) reports 70.6% on Verified using regression-test filtering plus a selector, and cautions that passing all regression tests neither guarantees correctness nor that a correct patch passes them all. All of this selects among independent attempts at a fresh issue, not among fixes to code that already has an open review finding.

sources.title: CodeMonkeys: Scaling Test-Time Compute for Software Engineering

claims.claim: Iterative LLM review-and-fix loops can add defects faster than they remove them (B01), and a test gate with rollback reduces this.
claims.what_sources_say: If It's Not Buggy, Don't Fix It (abstract fetched, 2026): across multiple models, the LLM claims bugs in bug-free programs, repair rate on buggy programs is lower than damage rate on correct ones, and edits fall into pseudo-cycles that add and remove the same change. No numbers on the page. Regression Accumulation in Multi-Turn Programming (abstract fetched, 2026): 542 tasks (HumanEval+, MBPP+), six LLMs, 8-turn chains; 40% to 73% of tasks lose previously correct behavior; a Verification Gate (run prior tests, roll back and retry) was the only strategy that helped every model, e.g. DeepSeek-V3 75.8% to 87.9% final-turn quality and Llama-3.1-8B 31.6% to 47.3%. A snippet of an ICLR 2026 Self-Refine paper says critics hallucinate flaws in correct code. These are function-level benchmarks, not a multi-module Django system, and the gate relies on pre-existing tests that cover the earlier behavior.

sources.title: If It's Not Buggy, Don't Fix It: On the Dynamics of Iterative Bug-fixing with LLMs
Regression Accumulation in Multi-Turn LLM Programming Conversations
Search results on iterative repair regression (ICLR 2026 Self-Refine snippet, ESEM 2026 IaC study)

claims.claim: There is direct evidence that generating several candidate fixes per review finding and selecting by executed tests (a tree or forest over fixes) reduces regression compared with one fix per round.
claims.what_sources_say: I found no study that measures this exact setup (multi-round review-driven fixing, N candidate fixes per finding, test-based selection, regression as the outcome). The nearest evidence is indirect: Agentless and CodeMonkeys show test-based selection among independent candidates raises resolve rate on fresh issues; Regression Accumulation shows a test gate with rollback and retry cuts regression on function-level tasks. Combined they make the idea plausible, not demonstrated. The value function matters: Agentless's generated tests were wrong a majority of the time (94 of 213 reproduction tests were valid), and Trae warns correct patches can fail stale regression tests. Tree search papers use LLM judges as value functions, which the 'Don't Fix It' result suggests are prone to false alarms.

sources.title: Regression Accumulation in Multi-Turn LLM Programming Conversations

claims.claim: Graph-of-Thoughts-style aggregation is a proven way to merge the outputs of parallel agents.
claims.what_sources_say: GoT's aggregation was measured on toy tasks such as sorting (abstract). No source I read measures aggregation of parallel coding agents' artifacts. The closest evidence: Parallel-Distill-Refine (abstract) distils parallel drafts into a bounded workspace and refines, with gains on AIME math; CodeMonkeys and Agentless pick among candidates rather than merge them. Merging code or documents is a different problem (conflicts, stale shared files) that ordinary version control and per-slice ownership address.

sources.title: Rethinking Thinking Tokens: LLMs as Improvement Operators

implications.implication: Evidence supports a narrow, cheap change: make every fix round pass a regression gate before it counts (run the full prior suite plus a test for the finding being fixed; roll back and retry on failure; cap rounds; stop when no new executable failure appears). This is the only mechanism with a measured regression reduction (Regression Accumulation, function-level benchmarks). Generating N candidate fixes and selecting by executed tests is plausible from Agentless/CodeMonkeys but not demonstrated for review-fix regressions; trial it on one slice and count new P1s per round against one-fix-per-round rather than adopting it. It does not support a full ToT/FoT tree, LLM-judge value functions, or more model-review rounds: the 'Don't Fix It' result says repeated LLM review invents defects and cycles. The B01 examples (permanent stock hold, lost restore point after rollback) are state and ordering bugs that only a test written for that invariant would catch; selection is only as good as the tests.

Executed tests are a stronger selector than model reading: in Agentless each added test-based filter raised resolve rate, and LLM-judge value functions (SWE-Search) have only self-reported relative gains. Evidence supports moving review weight from model reading to tests and runs. It does not support adding more model reviewers or debate; matched-compute work finds debate and Reflexion no better than self-consistency and sometimes worse as budget grows (math/QA, not code).

Nothing here shows that a tree or graph structure over the orchestrator's reviews reduces the serial gate. The structured-reasoning papers are about a single problem's answer, not about throughput. The one transferable idea is bounded distillation of parallel outputs into a small workspace (Parallel-Distill-Refine, math only), which resembles the orchestrator receiving short structured verdicts instead of long reports. Evidence does not support GoT as an orchestration architecture.

GoT aggregation was measured only on sorting-type tasks; no source shows it merging parallel agents' documents. Evidence supports nothing beyond ordinary practice (per-slice append-only fragments merged mechanically). Do not adopt GoT for shared-document merging on this evidence.

Selection by executed tests shows the value of checking claims mechanically: Agentless's generated reproduction tests were invalid in a majority of cases (94 of 213 valid), and Trae warns passing tests is not proof. Supports requiring that a report's test evidence be re-run by a script, not by another model reading it; it does not support LLM-judge or debate verification of reports.
This lane's evidence does not bear on it. Search over candidates cannot find a gap in what was never tested; the clean-install walk is an acceptance test, not a reasoning-method problem.

Tree, forest or best-of-n methods multiply tokens and calls (Agentless 40 patches per issue; CodeMonkeys about $2,300 for the Verified run), which makes the usage-limit problem worse. Use only in narrow places with a cap.

Candidate-fix selection by executed tests multiplies the number of checks run on the PC, which already queues behind itself (B06-B08). Evidence says the benefit exists only if the tests are fast and trustworthy; on this machine the cost would land in the bottleneck. Run candidates in a cheap, narrow test scope.

result.notes:
Verdicts per method. ToT: not worth its cost here (toy-task gains on GPT-4, 5-20x compute per secondary sources, no evidence it survives reasoning models). GoT: not worth it for merging agents; idea of aggregation only helps in a narrow place (distilling parallel candidates into a short workspace, math evidence). FoT: unverified (abstract only). Self-consistency / best-of-n with an executable verifier: helps in a narrow place, namely where a real test can select among candidates; it is the only family with coding evidence (Agentless, CodeMonkeys, Trae). MCTS coding agents (SWE-Search, CodeTree): not worth it yet; LLM value function, self-reported, no equal-cost comparison seen. Debate and Reflexion: not worth it; matched-compute study says they can degrade with more budget. LATS: not read at all (no primary or snippet evidence found). Reflexion HumanEval numbers only from a secondary summary, not used.

Could not read: full text of Forest-of-Thought, SWE-Search, CodeTree, CodeMonkeys, Parallel-Distill-Refine, Reasoning in Token Economies, and both 2026 regression papers (only abstracts, so no model lists or most numbers). The last 24k characters of the Agentless HTML were not read. A PDF fetch (arXiv 2503.14269) returned only compressed binary. Searches returned many blog and vendor pages (Trae blog, PatchFusion Codex blog, tutorials) that I treated as snippet-only or ignored. I made 15 WebFetch calls counting retries after an invalid-URL error (about 14 productive). Direct re-tests of ToT on reasoning models and cost-normalised ToT vs CoT studies were not found; absence in two searches is not proof none exist. Almost all coding evidence is 2024-2025 and the 2026 regression studies are function-level (HumanEval+/MBPP+); none is on a large multi-module app, so transfer to a Django clinic system is an inference. Needs research: the B01 candidate-fix experiment (a cheap in-house A/B on the clinic repo's logged review rounds is the right test). The conclusion on B01 comes from combining sources, not from one that measured it. Nothing was installed, run or changed in any repository; only the bottlenecks file was read.

result.topic: Lane B2: graph-structured memory and retrieval, and whether spatial/temporal topology in recall saves tokens (as of 2026-11-11)

claims.claim: Zep/Graphiti (bi-temporal knowledge graph) cuts context tokens and latency versus full-context while raising accuracy on LongMemEval.
claims.what_sources_say: Measured (LongMemEval, Table 2): full-context gpt-4o 60.2% at ~115k tokens, 28.9 s; Zep gpt-4o 71.2% at ~1.6k tokens, 2.58 s. gpt-4o-mini: 55.4% -> 63.8%. Bi-temporal: each edge carries valid time (t_valid/t_invalid) and transaction time (t'_created/t'_expired); a contradicting fact closes the old edge's validity. The comparison is against FULL CONTEXT, not against a tuned vector/BM25 retriever. Stated limits: single-session-assistant category regressed (-17.7 pts gpt-4o); weaker models may misread temporal data; authors could not run MemGPT on LongMemEval; DMR called a weak benchmark. Models are 2024-era gpt-4o; this predates current frontier models with large context. Zep is a vendor paper.

sources.title: Zep: A Temporal Knowledge Graph Architecture for Agent Memory (HTML)

claims.claim: Mem0 and Mem0-graph beat plain RAG on token/latency, and graph memory adds accuracy.
claims.what_sources_say: Measured (LoCoMo, GPT-4o-mini, Mem0 paper's own tables): Mem0 J=66.88, 1,764 memory tokens/query, p95 1.44 s; Mem0g (Neo4j graph) J=68.44, 3,616 tokens, p95 2.59 s; Zep 65.99, 3,911 tokens, 2.93 s; best RAG (2x256-token chunks) 60.97, <=512 tokens, 1.91 s; full-context 72.90, 26,031 tokens, 17.1 s. So the graph variant gains ~1.6 J points for about double the tokens and latency of flat Mem0 and is still below full context on accuracy. The paper says Zep's graph exceeds 600k tokens of footprint (Mem0 ~7k, Mem0g ~14k) and that Zep's async LLM graph build made immediate retrieval unreliable. These are the Mem0 authors' numbers about competitors.

sources.title: Mem0: Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory (HTML)

claims.claim: The agent-memory benchmark results (LoCoMo, DMR) are disputed and do not reliably rank graph memory above simple baselines.
claims.what_sources_say: Search snippets (secondary): Zep claimed 84% on LoCoMo, Mem0 re-ran it and reported 58.44% (alleging Zep included the adversarial category), Zep then published a corrected 75.14%; no independent party settled it. Letta reported that a plain filesystem agent (grep, open, search over files; gpt-4o-mini) scored 74.0% on LoCoMo, above Mem0's reported 68.5% graph score; self-reported, and Mem0 later claims 92.5% with a different pipeline and models, so numbers are not comparable. Commentators note full context (~73% J) beats Mem0g (~68%) because LoCoMo fits in a modern window, and that LoCoMo does not test knowledge updates. I did not read the primary Zep or Letta posts (snippet-only).

sources.title: Zep blog: Is Mem0 really SOTA in agent memory

claims.claim: Knowledge-graph RAG (GraphRAG, LightRAG, HippoRAG family) is not generally better than plain vector RAG; it helps on multi-hop/associative/global questions and costs much more to index.
claims.what_sources_say: HippoRAG 2 abstract (measured by its authors): +7% over the best embedding model on associative-memory tasks (personalised PageRank over a KG plus passages), while recent structure-augmented methods fall well short of standard RAG on simple factual QA; HippoRAG 2 itself claims to avoid that loss. Per-benchmark numbers and indexing cost not read (abstract only). GraphRAG-Bench abstract: GraphRAG frequently underperforms vanilla RAG on many real-world tasks; which tasks favour graphs is not stated on the page I read. Microsoft: LazyGraphRAG indexing costs 0.1% of full GraphRAG (same as vector RAG), implying full GraphRAG's LLM entity extraction is ~1000x vector indexing; vector RAG is best for local queries, GraphRAG global search targets whole-corpus questions. LightRAG and the original GraphRAG paper not read.

sources.title: When to use Graphs in RAG (GraphRAG-Bench)

claims.claim: A-MEM and MemGPT/Letta show self-organising or tiered memory improves agents.
claims.what_sources_say: Only a third-party number: in the Mem0 paper's LoCoMo table A-Mem scored 48.38 J at 2,520 tokens and p95 4.4 s, below plain RAG (60.97), and MemGPT/Letta's best public number is the filesystem-agent result above. I did not read the A-MEM or MemGPT papers.

claims.claim: Code-structure graphs (LocAgent: directory/file/class/function nodes; contain/import/invoke/inherit edges) improve localisation accuracy at lower cost.
claims.what_sources_say: Measured (SWE-Bench-Lite, 274 instances, file-level Acc@5; models 2024-era): BM25 61.7; best embedding (CodeRankEmbed) 84.7; Agentless 74.5-79.6; MoatlessTools 85.0-86.1; SWE-agent and OpenHands 69-74 with GPT-4o, 90.2 with Claude-3.5; LocAgent 94.2 with Claude-3.5, 92.7 with fine-tuned Qwen-32B. Cost per instance: LocAgent Claude-3.5 $0.66 (7 rounds) vs SWE-agent $0.67 (9 rounds), OpenHands $0.79 (13), MoatlessTools $0.46 (5); the large cost cut ($0.09) comes from the fine-tuned open 32B model, not from the graph. On Loc-Bench: LocAgent-Claude 83.4 vs OpenHands 79.8, SWE-agent 77.7, embedding 74.3. So the graph adds ~4 points over strong agentic baselines and about ties them on cost with the same model; the graph index takes seconds per repo. Python-only; no token counts reported.

sources.title: LocAgent: Graph-Guided LLM Agents for Code Localization (HTML)

claims.claim: RepoGraph (line-level call/def graph plug-in) raises SWE-bench resolve rates.
claims.what_sources_say: Abstract only: plugged into four methods of two approaches, it 'substantially boosts' all and sets a new open-source state of the art; also tested on CrossCodeEval. No resolve-rate numbers, models or costs obtained. CodexGraph, RepoHyper and KGCompass not read.

claims.claim: Aider's repo map (tree-sitter definitions/references, graph ranking, token-budgeted) is a measured token-saver.
claims.what_sources_say: Aider's own write-up describes the mechanism (file graph, ranking of most-referenced identifiers, --map-tokens default 1k) and reports no benchmark or numbers. It is a fixed-budget orientation map, not a measured saving. Aider's other published evaluations were not read.

sources.title: Building a better repository map with tree sitter (Aider)

claims.claim: Off-the-shelf code-graph MCP servers cut tokens by ~99% versus grep.
claims.what_sources_say: Snippet-level only. codebase-memory-mcp's 99.2% (3.4k vs 412k tokens) is a single vendor scenario against a naive file-by-file grep baseline; an independent reproduction noted the unoptimised baseline. LeanKG's own repo reports that token-saving claims were marketing, that it won F1 on 3 of 13 tests, and one A/B run had the graph arm using MORE tokens (191k vs 150k, 7-test average); another with 4 runs per arm showed 7 vs 9 tool calls and $0.37 vs $0.53. Small samples, vendor-run.

sources.title: codebase-memory-mcp speeds AI coding agent queries

claims.claim: Temporal/history retrieval (commit history, co-change) helps coding agents localise.
claims.what_sources_say: Measured (RepoMem on LocAgent, GPT-4o, file-level, ICLR 2026): SWE-bench-verified Acc@5 71.6 -> 76.5 (+4.9), Acc@1 64.8 -> 68.6; SWE-bench-live subset Acc@5 63.1 -> 66.2. Memory = 7,000 prior commits (episodic) + 200 cached file summaries (semantic). Gains concentrate in repos with rich history (pytest +16.7, sphinx +11.4, django +7.4); repos with under 10k commits LOST 13.1 points on average, so a young repo may not benefit. Staleness and recency effects were not analysed; function-level not reported; no token numbers. HAFixAgent (snippet): history helps bug repair on Defects4J/BugsInPy without raising steps/tokens significantly. I found no measured study of co-change mining or decay for coding agents.

sources.title: Improving Code Localization with Repository Memory (HTML)

claims.claim: Claude Code dropped pre-built indexes for agentic search (grep/read on demand) and Anthropic gives reasons.
claims.what_sources_say: Primary (Latent Space interview with Claude Code's creator, 2025): early versions used RAG over an off-the-shelf embedding index; agentic search 'outperformed everything. By a lot', but the evaluation was admitted to be 'just vibes, so internal vibes'. Stated reasons: index goes stale as code drifts; hosting an index is a security issue; trade-off is more latency and tokens. So it is a design choice with unpublished evidence, not a measured result, and it concedes token cost. Secondary write-ups say RAG may still win on huge repos and concept search; the turbopuffer talk says it does not prove semantic retrieval is unsuitable. No source found giving a repo size at which a graph starts to pay. Last 13k characters of the interview were not read.

sources.title: Dev.to: The representation problem, RAG vs agentic search

claims.claim: Kuzu is no longer a safe embedded graph store; sqlite-vec is pre-v1 with thin upstream maintenance; SQLite recursive CTEs can serve as a graph store.
claims.what_sources_say: Kuzu: GitHub repo archived 2025-10-10 after Apple's acquisition (snippet-level, several news sources); last release 0.11.3, forks exist (e.g. ArcadeDB markets a migration path, vendor claim). sqlite-vec: README states pre-v1 with possible breaking changes; no visible 2026 upstream activity found, community forks (one PhotoStructure-funded) carry maintenance. Recursive CTE traversal and simple-graph were NOT researched or fetched; WITH RECURSIVE is core SQLite, but I have no measured performance or no benchmark at this owner's scale.

claims.claim: Graph maintenance cost and staleness under hundreds of commits a week, and incremental update approaches, are well characterised.
claims.what_sources_say: I found no measured study. Indirect evidence only: Claude Code's creator cites staleness as a reason to drop indexes; LocAgent says a code graph builds in seconds per repo (so rebuild-from-source is cheap for deterministic AST graphs); Mem0 says Zep's LLM-built graph ran async multi-call construction and was unreliable for immediate retrieval; LazyGraphRAG shows LLM-extracted graphs cost ~1000x vector indexing. RepoMem did not analyse staleness. Incremental update claims (Graphiti incremental ingestion, per-file tree-sitter reparse) were not verified.

implications.implication: This is where recall plausibly cuts tokens: the orchestrator's context overflows and is summarised. The only strong measured token result for graph/temporal memory is Zep-style retrieval versus FULL context (115k -> 1.6k tokens, accuracy up) and Mem0 (26k -> 1.8k, accuracy down ~6 points). Evidence supports a small, deterministic, queryable store of decisions, slice status and gate verdicts (facts with valid-from and superseded-at) that the orchestrator queries instead of rereading the board. It does not show that graph structure beats a flat indexed table or FTS/BM25; the comparison against a tuned flat baseline is missing, and Letta's filesystem result suggests flat can match. Use a flat bi-temporal fact table first; add graph edges only if a query needs a multi-hop join.

Shared documents with one writer (800-line board, stale AGENTS.md and context map) are a validity-time problem: Zep's model (close an old fact's validity when a new one contradicts it) fits, and it avoids stale text being read. Evidence is from conversational memory, not engineering documents. It supports generating the board and context map as views over an append-only, per-slice-written event/fact table, not graph recall per se. No measured result for this use.

Graphs do not fix overstated reports. LLM-extracted graphs add extraction errors (GraphRAG-Bench: graph RAG often underperforms vanilla RAG; Zep regressions in some categories). Facts that gate decisions (test existed, command exit code) should be recorded by the harness from deterministic tool output, then recalled; evidence does not support letting a model extract them from prose into a graph.

Fix rounds that create new defects are a localisation and blast-radius problem. Deterministic code graphs (imports, callers, co-change) give a measured localisation gain over strong agentic baselines (LocAgent +4 pts Acc@5 on SWE-Bench-Lite, +3.6 on Loc-Bench; RepoMem history +4.9 pts) on Python benchmarks with 2024-era models. This supports an inexpensive callers/co-changed-files report attached to each fix round as a reviewer checklist. It does not show fewer new P1s; nobody measured regressions introduced per fix round. The clinic repo is Django (rich history helps; RepoMem django +7.4) but is only nine days old, and RepoMem lost 13 points on repos with under 10k commits, so history features may not help yet.

Nothing in this lane bears on the clean-install gap; it is an end-to-end acceptance test problem, not a recall problem. A graph would not have found a missing seeder step. Do not spend research on graphs for it.

Token and memory use per idle session: a deterministic index can be a single SQLite file read by many sessions, avoiding per-session context rebuilding and avoiding a graph server (Neo4j-class) that would add to memory pressure. Evidence is design reasoning plus Mem0g's doubled latency/tokens versus flat Mem0; no measured RAM comparison. Avoid Kuzu (repo archived Oct 2025) and treat sqlite-vec as pre-v1; FTS5/BM25 plus recursive CTEs need no extension.

Resumability after a halt is a state-persistence benefit of an on-disk memory store (recall survives session death), and Letta/Zep both frame memory as durable. No measured evidence on resumption quality; the stronger fix is committed state files that a fresh session can read, whatever the store.

Long subagent reports flow through the orchestrator's context. A shared store where subagents write structured findings (by id) and the orchestrator reads only ids and summaries is consistent with the measured Mem0/Zep pattern (retrieve ~2k tokens, not ~26-115k). Not measured for subagent reports; and since subagents cannot write files, the orchestrator or a tool wrapper would have to do the write, which re-enters its context.

Carrying dozens of P3 findings is a recency and validity matter (which are still open, which were superseded by later commits). A temporal fact table fits, but there is no measured benefit; a status column and an auto-close-on-touch rule is the plain version.

Not addressed by this lane. A caution only: LLM-built graph indexing (full GraphRAG about 1000x vector indexing cost per Microsoft) and graph databases would add load on a PC already under memory pressure; deterministic tree-sitter/AST indexing (seconds per repo per LocAgent) does not.

Not addressed directly. Agentic grep search costs tokens and latency, per Anthropic's own admission; a prebuilt index would cut exploration turns but does not reduce check queueing. No measurement links the two.

Four early fetches failed on a missing URL scheme and were retried. The fetch tool summarises pages with a small model, so table numbers are as relayed by that summariser, not re-checked against the PDFs.

NOT READ / SNIPPET-ONLY: the primary Zep rebuttal and the Mem0 GitHub issue on LoCoMo (the 84%/58.44%/75.14% figures are from secondary snippets and unresolved); the Letta filesystem post (74.0% vs 68.5% from a snippet); the original GraphRAG, LightRAG, HippoRAG (v1), A-MEM, MemGPT, CodexGraph, RepoHyper, KGCompass papers; HippoRAG 2 and GraphRAG-Bench result tables and indexing costs (abstracts only); Sourcegraph SCIP/Cody context and any Cody statement on dropping embeddings; code property graphs; Graphiti's incremental-ingestion docs; SQLite WITH RECURSIVE and simple-graph (no research done); Kuzu archival and sqlite-vec state are from search snippets; code-graph MCP token claims are vendor snippets. I could not find: a repo size at which a code graph starts to pay; measured co-change mining or decay for coding agents; any study of graph staleness at hundreds of commits per week; any benchmark of a graph versus a tuned grep agent measuring resolved rate and tokens with 2025-2026 frontier models. Most measured code results use GPT-4o or Claude-3.5 (2024) and Python SWE-bench repos, so they predate current frontier models whose agentic search is likely stronger; effects of graphs on them may be smaller.

VERDICT (per the brief). Where graph recall likely cuts tokens: (a) orchestrator and cross-session state (B04, B13, B16): replacing re-reading of long boards and reports with queried facts, with the best-supported pattern being bi-temporal facts (valid-from/superseded) retrieved at ~1.6-3.6k tokens instead of 26-115k; (b) fix-round blast-radius lookups (B01) via deterministic import/caller/co-change queries. Unproven: that a GRAPH (rather than a flat FTS5/BM25 table with a few join tables) beats a flat store for these jobs; that code graphs reduce tokens for a current frontier agent already using grep; that history features help a nine-day-old repo; any gain on B02, B05, B07, B12. 'Spatial and temporal topology saves tokens' is supported only in the narrow form: retrieval beats stuffing full context; it is not shown to beat well-tuned flat retrieval or agentic search.

ONE DECIDING MEASUREMENT: replay N (about 30) real orchestrator or reviewer tasks from the clinic repo's own git and session history (for example, 'which files and open findings does this fix round touch', 'what was decided about X and is it still true'), run each with three arms using the same current model: (A) plain agentic grep/read plus the existing board, (B) SQLite FTS5 plus a bi-temporal fact table, (C) B plus a deterministic tree-sitter import/caller/co-change edge table via recursive CTEs. Record total input+output tokens, tool calls, wall time, and answer correctness checked against the git history. Adopt C only if it beats B on tokens at equal correctness, and B only if it beats A. Cost: a day of work, no new dependencies, no installs."

Small samples, weak open-weight models, one benchmark, so the direction is informative and the magnitudes are not transferable to frontier models. A Kozuchi-agent paper (search snippet only) reports regressions as only about 5% of failures, with wrong fix about 91%, so regressions are not the dominant failure of single patches. claims.what_sources_say: arXiv 2609.10123 (Sep 2026, 'If It's Not Buggy, Don't Fix It') reports, per its abstract only: LLMs claim to find bugs in bug-free programs, repair rate on buggy programs is lower than damage rate on correct programs, and a pseudo-cycle appears where the same changes are added and removed. The abstract gives no numbers, models or benchmarks, proposes no tested mitigation, and says it bears on stopping conditions. I read only the abstract. This is the closest direct evidence for B01 but its effect size is unknown.

claims.what_sources_say: Shukla et al. (IEEE ISTAS 2025) MEASURED: 400 code samples, 40 rounds, four prompting strategies; 37.6% more critical vulnerabilities after five rounds (models unnamed on the abstract page; 2025-era models). SCAFFOLD-CEGIS (Mar 2026) MEASURED with GPT-4o over 10 rounds: 43.7% of iteration chains ended with more vulnerabilities than the baseline; SAST gating raised latent degradation from 12.5% to 20.8% (static rules miss removed defensive logic and weakened exception handling); the authors' own constraint-based method cut it to 2.1% (self-reported, authors' benchmark). Both are preprints/workshop-level, security-specific, and use older models; generalising to correctness bugs is inference.

I did not fetch GitClear's own report (secondary coverage only). Weak support for B01; do not base harness decisions on it.

claims.what_sources_say: Evidence is on test generation quality, not on loop convergence. SWT-Bench line MEASURED fail-to-pass rates for generated reproduction tests: Otter 31.4% to 37.0% on SWT-Verified; adding existing regression tests as context 31.2% to 34.0% (Claude 3.7 Sonnet); AssertFlip 43.6%; e-Otter++ 63% on TDD-Bench Verified (not comparable). The search found no result showing that these tests raise final agent resolution rates; e-Otter++'s abstract only argues issues are easier to resolve with a reproduction test. So the fail-before/pass-after practice is well-founded as a verification oracle but its effect on convergence is unmeasured here. All snippet-only.

claims.what_sources_say: Property-based: agentic Hypothesis-writing agent over 100 Python packages (Maaz et al., Oct 2025): 56% of reports valid bugs, 32% worth reporting to maintainers, top-ranked 21 reports 86% valid; 5 bugs reported, 3 patches merged (model unnamed on page; fetched abstract). It finds library bugs; it was not tested on review-fix convergence. Mutation: Meta ACH (FSE'25, snippet only) 571 tests across 10,795 Kotlin classes, 73% accepted by engineers, 277 would have been dropped by a coverage criterion; MUTGEN snippet reports suites with 100% coverage but 4% mutation score. These show tests can look good while being weak, which supports a mutation check on the tests written per finding, but I found no measurement of mutation gating inside an AI repair loop.

claims.claim: A reviewer from a different model family catches defects the first misses.
claims.what_sources_say: Two conflicting small studies. Stone (Zenodo preprint, Jun 2026, single team, not peer reviewed) MEASURED 18 artifacts, 154 confirmed issues, eight model versions from five providers: no model above about 64% recall on code; 56.5% of defects found by exactly one model; coverage rose from 33.6% to 57.1% on adding a second vendor's model; author calls it directional. Song (arXiv 2610.01471, Oct 2026, single author, 30 artifacts with 150 PLANTED errors, 900 sessions, models unnamed): top-tier cross-model review did not differ significantly from a same-model fresh-session review in F1 (not shown equivalent); the two found partly different errors (Jaccard 41.2%); one fresh-session plus one cross-model review matched more errors than two fresh-session reviews (56.7% vs 42.7%, p=.006) but not more than two cross-model reviews, so vendor difference is confounded with capability. Net: independent multiple reviews beat one; whether the second must be another vendor is unsettled. Neither measures review of fixes in a loop.

Those are practitioner advice, plausible by construction (the clinic failures, real data refused and no till creation on a fresh install, are exactly what a clean-install journey test would hit), but unmeasured.

implications.implication: SUPPORTS: treat every fix as a new patch that must be separately verified, not as a reviewed edit. Per finding, write a failing reproduction test first, require it to pass after, and run the tests selected by the fix's dependency impact (TDAD-style) plus the full existing suite; the evidence says tests are the oracle and model reading is not enough (7.8%/29.6% wrong-but-passing, damage rate above repair rate in 2609.10123). Cap rounds and escalate to a human or a different reviewer once a round's fix touches code that an earlier round already changed (the pseudo-cycle signature). Add a mutation check (or manual fault-injection) on the new test for money, stock and restore paths. DOES NOT SUPPORT: any claim that a given round cap (2, 3, 4) or batching-versus-serial policy is optimal, since nothing measured those; do not expect prompts like 'follow TDD' to help by themselves (9.94% regressions in TDAD). Effect sizes come from older or small open-weight models, so measure on the clinic repo's own round history before trusting them.

SUPPORTS: FeatureBench (11.0% vs 74.4%) shows unit-level success does not predict feature-level success, so a standing gate is justified: a golden-path journey test on a clean install with an empty database (create till, create account, import real-shaped data, take a sale, close day), run in CI from slice 1 and extended each slice, plus a seed that is a sample of real data shapes rather than a seeder written by the same agent. DOES NOT SUPPORT: citing evidence that walking skeletons, tracer bullets or deployment rehearsal reduce late gaps; none was found, this is practitioner advice. Cheap to do, so evidence need not block it. Research need: low.

SUPPORTS: the wrong-but-passing results (7.8% fail the real suite, 29.6% diverge) and the METR gap mean a report claiming 'tests pass' is weak evidence. Require reports to cite a runnable test id that the harness executes and that fails on the pre-fix commit, rather than prose. Reviewer verification of this can be mechanical. DOES NOT SUPPORT any figure for how often agent reports overstate; none measured.

SUPPORTS some independent review, not a rate. Human maintainers rejected a substantial share of grader-passing patches, but a model-versus-human reviewer comparison was not found, and the rubber-stamping evidence is secondary. Sensible design: use model reviewers for breadth (two reviews beat one; multi-family reviews found different defects in two small studies), and reserve human attention for the highest-risk surfaces (money, stock, restore, auth, migrations, data import) by sampling, scoped to the risk, with fresh independent reviewers rather than a fixed percentage. Do not claim a vendor split is required: the controlled planted-error study found no significant F1 difference between a fresh same-model session and a cross-model one, whereas the one-team study found a large gain; both small. A cheap hedge is one different-family reviewer on the high-risk slices only.

No evidence found either way. Rerunning the 12-user load test after every query or schema change as a CI or pre-merge gate is practitioner advice and cheap relative to the cost of a stale result; add a concurrency test for the stock and cutoff paths where the review-fix loop already produced bugs. Research need: low, mostly an engineering decision for the owner.

No evidence found on bug-debt policies for AI-built code. The only measurement found (OSS-Fuzz) shows low-impact bugs tend to stay open for a long time. A defensible policy is one the owner sets: tag each carried P3 with the code path and slice, fail the pilot gate if a P3 touches money, stock, auth or data import (re-triage), and re-triage the list at each release. This is judgment, not evidence.

Evidence lane does not measure Windows-vs-Linux, but the pattern in B02 and the 'tests pass vs works' gap support making the Linux container run (matching production) the gate, with the Windows run advisory. Treat as engineering inference.

claims.claim: 1a. Kernel-Power Event 41 with BugcheckCode 0 and PowerButtonTimestamp 0 means no crash code was written: power loss, hard hang or hard reset, not a recorded memory-exhaustion stop. A nonzero BugcheckCode (logged in decimal) means a bugcheck occurred and should be converted to hex and decoded.
claims.what_sources_say: Microsoft's archived TechNet wiki defines Event 41 as 'rebooted without cleanly shutting down' and splits it into three scenarios: (1) nonzero BugcheckCode, written in decimal so convert to hex; (2) power button held 4+ seconds, so PowerButtonTimestamp is nonzero; (3) both zero, which it ties to power loss or a hard hang and says 'usually indicates' hardware and/or driver problems. It lists these checks: disable overclocking, run a memory checker, confirm PSU wattage is enough for the installed parts, check temperatures. Nothing in it says memory exhaustion produces code 0. A search snippet showed one low-quality site claiming a MEMORY_MANAGEMENT stop can give code 0; that conflicts with the Microsoft page. The page is archived (updated 2024) and written for Windows 6.1-era behaviour. It predates the 2026 builds, though the event semantics are stable. NOTHING MEASURED here; it is guidance.

sources.title: Kernel Power Event ID 41 (Microsoft Learn, archived TechNet wiki)
Search results: Event 41 BugcheckCode 0 (Microsoft Q&A, ManageEngine)

claims.claim: 1b. Windows does not power the machine off when memory is exhausted; commit-limit exhaustion makes allocations fail and is reported as Resource-Exhaustion-Detector Event 2004, with the top three commit consumers named. A clean power-off or reset during memory pressure therefore points to something else (hang, hardware, thermal, PSU, driver) or an actual bugcheck.
claims.what_sources_say: Microsoft-origin material surfaced only as search snippets: Event 2004 is logged by the Resource Exhaustion Detector when commit charge reaches a critical level and lists the top three committed-memory consumers; the commit limit is set by RAM plus pagefile, so a small or disabled pagefile hits it sooner; one source gives roughly 80 percent commit/limit as the 'insufficient memory' signal (a rule of thumb, not Microsoft-measured); one Microsoft Q&A answer cautions that the listed processes are often victims, not the cause. I did not find a page stating outright 'Windows never powers off on memory exhaustion'. That is inferred from the 2004 mechanism and from Microsoft's Event 41 guidance, which names no memory-exhaustion path to a code-0 reboot. Russinovich's 'Pushing the Limits of Windows: Virtual Memory' was NOT found, so the commit-limit definition is secondhand. Bug check 0x9E (USER_MODE_HEALTH_MONITOR, fetched) is the one documented watchdog bugcheck tied to resource starvation, but it concerns cluster/server components and is unlikely on a Windows 11 desktop.

claims.claim: 2a. WSL2 .wslconfig [wsl2] defaults in 2026: memory = 50% of Windows RAM; processors = all logical; swap = 25% of memory rounded up to the nearest GB (swapFile %Temp%\swap.vhdx); vmIdleTimeout 60000 ms (Windows 11 only); [experimental] autoMemoryReclaim default dropCache (values disabled|gradual|dropCache); sparseVhd default false; changes need wsl --shutdown and about 8 seconds.

The page recommends editing through the WSL Settings app. New keys listed include maxCrashDumpCount (10), crashDumpFolder (%Temp%\wsl-crashes), defaultVhdSize (1 TB), instanceIdleTimeout (15000 ms, in [general]), and an experimental virtiofs boolean (default false, needs virtio and hostFileSystemAccess). Idle PostgreSQL costs: each container carries its own shared_buffers (default 128MB, reserved as shared memory and touched as used), work_mem 4MB, maintenance_work_mem 64MB per backend where used; 26 database containers therefore plausibly cost on the order of a few GB at idle, and consolidating onto one server or lowering shared_buffers cuts that.

The docs give no idle-footprint measurement. claims.claim: 3c. Non-durable Postgres settings speed up a throwaway test database: fsync=off, synchronous_commit=off, full_page_writes=off, larger max_wal_size and checkpoint_timeout, unlogged tables, or the data directory on a RAM disk (tmpfs).
claims.what_sources_say: PostgreSQL docs (Non-Durable Settings, fetched) list exactly these six. Durability still holds if only the database software crashes. No speedup figure is given in the docs. Suitable only for disposable test databases, never for the backup-bearing or production data. docker compose watch, in-container test runners and sync were not fetched in this lane.

claims.claim: 4a. Database-per-worker for pytest-xdist: pytest-django suffixes the test database name per xdist worker so workers do not interfere; --reuse-db keeps the database between runs (it does not detect schema changes, so --create-db after changes); --no-migrations builds from models; a template database (CREATE DATABASE ... TEMPLATE) can be wired by overriding django_db_setup.
claims.what_sources_say: pytest-django docs (fetched) state all of this; the page does not show the exact suffix, so 'gw0' naming is not confirmed there. pytest-xdist docs (fetched) give the worker_id fixture (e.g. 'gw2', 'master' when not distributed), PYTEST_XDIST_WORKER and PYTEST_XDIST_WORKER_COUNT env vars, testrun_uid for naming per-run resources, and a FileLock pattern in the shared temp dir to run a session fixture once across workers. The xdist page did not cover -n auto, -n logical or --dist loadscope/loadgroup; I did not fetch the CLI reference. Not found: any measured per-worker memory or any benchmark of one shared Postgres with many databases versus one container per check. Reasoning (mine, unmeasured): one shared server with many databases avoids N copies of shared_buffers and background processes; separate containers give isolation of crashes and resources.

claims.claim: 5a. Restart policies: unless-stopped and always restart containers when the Docker daemon starts; no (default) and on-failure do not; unless-stopped keeps manually stopped containers stopped. For Docker Desktop on Windows the daemon only starts when Docker Desktop starts, which is a separate setting ('Start Docker Desktop when you sign in', off by default).
claims.what_sources_say: Docker engine docs (fetched): no is default; on-failure does not restart after a daemon restart; always restarts whenever it stops, and after a manual stop only when the daemon restarts; unless-stopped is like always but a manually stopped container stays stopped. The page does not mention Docker Desktop. Docker settings page (fetched): 'Start Docker Desktop when you sign in' is off by default. Windows auto-login is needed for this to work after a reboot with nobody present (my inference; an auto-login or a service-level path is not documented in what I fetched). WSL2 systemd route: wsl.conf [boot] systemd=true (Windows 11, WSL from the Store; default false) and [boot] command= run as root, per Microsoft's page. A Task Scheduler task as an alternative was not fetched or verified.

claims.claim: 5b. A watchdog for a hung check: pytest-timeout with timeout = N and timeout_method = thread, which dumps all threads' stacks and then terminates the whole process; the signal method (default where SIGALRM exists) fails only the one test and continues.
claims.what_sources_say: pytest-timeout README (fetched): signal method is the default when SIGALRM is supported, dumps other threads' stacks and calls pytest.fail so the run continues; thread method is 'the surest and most portable', is the default where signal is unsupported, on expiry prints stacks of all threads and ends the process through os._exit() so teardown and JUnit XML are not written; thread has higher per-test overhead. Configuration: [pytest] timeout = 300, timeout_method = thread; PYTEST_TIMEOUT env var overrides ini; --timeout and --timeout-method override both; @pytest.mark.timeout(60, method="thread") per test; timeout_func_only=true excludes fixtures. The page does not name Windows; that Windows lacks SIGALRM (so thread is used) is my knowledge, not from the page. faulthandler_timeout was not covered by the fetched page, so it is unverified here. The Windows hang of 600 s was a whole-check hang including container startup, which a per-test timeout does not cover; an outer wrapper timeout is needed (my inference).

claims.claim: 6a. Off-machine copy with no remote: git bundle create backup.bundle --all packs all refs and reachable commits; git bundle verify checks it; git clone backup.bundle restores; incremental bundles use a range such as lastTag..master. A bundle excludes index, working tree, stash, per-repo config and hooks.
claims.what_sources_say: From the official git-bundle documentation (fetched): create with --all, verify with git bundle verify (nonzero exit when invalid or prerequisites missing), clone from the bundle, incremental flow with a tag marking the last bundled commit, other range forms (v1.0.0..master, --since, -N), list-heads, and read-only on the recipient side. Because the bundle excludes stash, config and hooks, uncommitted work and git stash would not be saved. Worktree-specific state is also not in the bundle.

claims.claim: 6b. Cost options for the off-machine copy: a private GitHub repository is free with unlimited collaborators but with limited private-repo features; restic or rclone to Backblaze B2 or Cloudflare R2 (about 10 GB free each, client-side encrypted by restic); a bare repository on a VPS over SSH has a VPS cost.
claims.what_sources_say: All from secondary sources and search snippets, not pricing pages: GitHub Free permits unlimited private repositories and collaborators with fewer features (no protected branches or required reviewers on private repos; one low-quality site claimed a 5-collaborator cap, contradicting GitHub's own plan docs, which were for Enterprise Server). Restic's S3 backend covers B2, R2 and S3 and encrypts and deduplicates client-side; both B2 and R2 report about 10 GB free; storage prices quoted (~$0.006/GB-month B2, ~$0.015 R2) vary between blogs. Trade-offs I can state from the sources: GitHub gives a real remote plus history but the code leaves the machine into a third party's custody (privacy, and a push uses the owner's credentials; an agent must not be handed those); restic or bundles to encrypted object storage keep contents unreadable to the provider but need a key backup and a restore test; a VPS is more setup than the other two. A current official pricing page for each was not read. Repository size matters: a 430-commit, nine-day Django repo is likely well under any free tier, but I measured nothing.

implications.implication: Evidence supports a staged diagnosis, not a guess. Step 1: in the System log pull Events 41, 6008, 1074, 6005/6006, 1001 and Event 2004 for the two crash times. If 41 shows BugcheckCode 0 and PowerButtonTimestamp 0 with no 1001 and no minidump, Microsoft's page points at power loss, hard hang, hardware or driver, not at a recorded memory-exhaustion stop; if BugcheckCode is nonzero, convert decimal to hex and decode it. Step 2: check WHEA-Logger events, temperatures under load, PSU wattage versus parts, overclock/XMP state, and run a memory test (the Microsoft page lists all four). Step 3: bound the memory side by setting .wslconfig memory and swap explicitly instead of the 50% default so Windows keeps headroom, and check pagefile is system-managed so the commit limit is not tiny. What the evidence does NOT support: asserting that memory pressure caused the shutdowns. Windows is documented to report commit exhaustion as Event 2004, not to power off, so the memory theory is plausible only as a trigger of a hang or driver fault. Whether a hang under WSL2 memory pressure can freeze the host is not covered by anything I read.

Microsoft and Docker both say to put the repository inside the WSL2 Linux filesystem and bind-mount from there, with databases in named volumes, and that Windows-path bind mounts are the slow path. That matches B06 and justifies making the Linux-container run the gate on a repo cloned into ext4 (also helps B18 since production is Linux). Evidence does not give a trustworthy ratio for a Django/Postgres suite: the only head-to-head numbers are an npm blog test (about 18x derived) and an old Docker issue (about 9.5x). Measure first: time the same pytest run from /mnt/c and from /home with hyperfine. Also unmeasured: tmpfs or fsync=off for the test Postgres (documented as safe only for disposable data) and the experimental virtiofs flag.

Queueing is a capacity-planning problem the sources only partly address. xdist per-worker databases (pytest-django suffixes names; worker_id and PYTEST_XDIST_WORKER_COUNT available) let one check use many CPUs, and --reuse-db or a CREATE DATABASE ... TEMPLATE copy cuts setup time per worker. For several checks at once, one shared Postgres server hosting many databases is cheaper in memory than a container per check, but no source measured that, and per-worker memory was not found. The 8 GB-free gate for a second slot should be replaced by measured numbers: run one check, record peak memory and wall time, then set slot count from that. Evidence does not support a specific worker count for 24 logical CPUs.

Documented levers: set .wslconfig [wsl2] memory (default 50% of RAM, 31 GB gives about 15.5 GB) and swap (default 25% of memory); [experimental] autoMemoryReclaim (default dropCache per the 2026 page) returns cached memory; sparseVhd shrinks disk; vmIdleTimeout (60000 ms) and Docker Resource Saver only act when idle, so they do nothing while 26 containers run. The Postgres defaults (shared_buffers 128MB, work_mem 4MB, maintenance_work_mem 64MB) mean each container is sized for a server; fewer containers or a lower shared_buffers is the documented direction. Not supported: any idle-memory figure for Postgres or for Claude sessions; measure with docker stats and Task Manager before cutting. The 20 idle sessions are outside this lane's evidence.

pytest-timeout (timeout and timeout_method = thread in pytest.ini, PYTEST_TIMEOUT env var, per-test marker) gives a documented watchdog that prints all thread stacks and exits, which would turn the next unexplained hang into a stack trace. Caveats from the README: thread method skips teardown and XML output. A 600 s hang that may sit in container startup, docker exec or the file boundary is not covered by a per-test timeout, so also wrap the whole check in an outer timeout and capture docker ps and docker logs on expiry (my inference, no source). Cause remains unknown; the evidence only supports making the next hang diagnosable, not explaining the last.

Two documented pieces: Docker's 'Start Docker Desktop when you sign in' setting (off by default) and container restart policies, where unless-stopped or always bring containers back when the daemon starts while no and on-failure do not. Together they cover the manual start, provided a user session logs in after reboot. Auto-login, a Task Scheduler task, and the WSL2 route (wsl.conf [boot] systemd=true or command=) are partly supported: the WSL settings are documented, the Task Scheduler and auto-login steps were not verified. Checks should still start their own database if it is missing, so they work even if the restart policy did not fire.

Cheapest working path from the sources: git bundle create <file> --all (official docs) written to a cloud-synced folder or pushed with restic/rclone to an encrypted bucket; git bundle verify and a test clone prove it restores. A private GitHub repo is free with unlimited collaborators per GitHub's plan docs and gives a real remote, at the cost of third-party custody and needing a credential, which agents should not hold. Bundles do not capture stash, hooks, config or uncommitted work, so commit or stash-to-branch first. Pricing and free tiers came from secondary sources; confirm on official pages. A scheduled run (Task Scheduler) is not verified here.
