result.topic: Lane B5: what Claude Code itself offers for process bottlenecks B03, B04, B12, B14, B15, B16 (official docs, read 2026-11-11)

claims.claim: (1a) After a usage limit halts a session, an open interactive session waits and continues by itself after reset (autoContinueAtUsageLimit; v2.1.234+).
claims.what_sources_say: In an interactive session signed in with a claude.ai subscription, auto-continue is on by default. It continues after the reset and does not resend the last message. Keep the session open. If the PC slept more than about 30 minutes and the limit reset meanwhile, you must press Enter. It stops after three automatic continuations (also for /goal and session-scoped scheduled tasks), when the reset is over 24 hours away, when you exit (the wait does not restart on resume), or when the session is moved to a background session, Desktop or the cloud. Permission prompts still stop the continued task while you are away. Not stated as supported for claude -p.

sources.title: Interactive mode: Wait for a usage limit to reset

claims.claim: (1b) Workflow runs pause at a usage limit and resume themselves (v2.1.271+; agent-level resume of failed agents v2.1.318+).
claims.what_sources_say: Agents that hit the limit wait for the reset and then run again; no new agents start meanwhile. Conditions: claude.ai subscription without usage-based billing; interactive terminal session or a local Desktop Code-tab session (the app must stay open); autoContinueAtUsageLimit on; reset within 24 hours (a weekly limit can be further out); at most two waits per run, the third hit fails the agent. No pause in claude -p, the Agent SDK, background sessions, Remote Control, agent-team teammates, SSH/WSL, Dispatch or scheduled-task sessions. A stopped or failed run is resumed by asking Claude to relaunch the workflow. Completed agents return saved results; a script edit reruns later agents.

sources.title: Workflows: When a run hits your usage limit

claims.claim: (1c) Scheduled tasks, /loop and ScheduleWakeup can resume work with the user absent, locally and in the cloud.
claims.what_sources_say: Three tiers are documented. Cloud scheduled tasks (formerly routines, research preview) need no machine or open session; minimum 1 hour; schedule, API or GitHub triggers; fresh clone, so no local files; auto mode by default; 100 scheduled runs per hour per account. When the subscription limit is hit, they run on metered overage only if usage credits are on; otherwise extra runs are rejected until the window resets. Desktop scheduled tasks need the machine on but no open session. /loop, CronCreate and ScheduleWakeup are session-scoped: they fire only while Claude Code is running and idle, expire after 7 days, and have no catch-up for missed fires. A self-paced loop is not restored on --resume. Backgrounding a session carries /loop tasks over to a background session; a background self-paced loop stops if its process is down when the wakeup falls due. The docs do not describe any trigger that resumes a session halted by a limit other than the auto-continue above.

sources.title: Cloud scheduled tasks (routines): Usage and limits

claims.claim: (1d) Background sessions (claude --bg, agent view) keep running without a terminal and across PC sleep, but not across a restart.
claims.what_sources_say: A separate supervisor process runs them. Sleep does not stop them and the supervisor reconnects on wake. A shutdown or restart stops running sessions: those waiting on you stay under Needs input; others show failed (progress within 48 hours) or stopped, and attach or reply restarts one from the saved conversation. Idle sessions unattached for about an hour have their process stopped, and pinning with Ctrl+T keeps one running. This bears on B05 and B10: after an unclean shutdown nothing restarts by itself. Cloud sessions continue when the computer is off (Desktop page). The page's usage-limit section was cut off, so session behavior at a limit is not confirmed. The workflows page says a background session does not pause a workflow at a limit.

claims.claim: (1e) /goal keeps a session working until a condition is met; claude -p and Remote Control are ways to drive sessions without sitting at the PC.
claims.what_sources_say: /goal is confirmed to exist (docs map: keep a session running until a condition is met); the interactive-mode page counts goal continuations in the three-continuation auto-continue cap. I did not fetch the goal page, so its details are unverified. The scheduled-tasks page also points to Channels for pushing CI events into a session. claude -p and Remote Control were not fetched; the workflows page only shows that a workflow run does not pause at a limit in those modes.

sources.title: Docs map (goal, headless, remote-control, channels pages listed)

claims.claim: (2) A session cannot start other sessions unless the user's message began the turn; there are supported ways to chain work without the user.
claims.what_sources_say: I found no such documented rule on the Desktop page. The page describes suggested-task cards where Start 'starts the task in another session', which implies a user click, and Dispatch spawning sessions. Related documented facts: scheduled-task prompts are not live user input and cannot act as approval or consent; the ultracode keyword works only in typed prompts; sessions that bypass permission prompts hold incoming peer messages for approval by default. The user-turn rule may be an app-level guard not covered by these pages; the unread tail of the Desktop page might hold it. Supported chaining without a user: workflows (a script launches subagents in one session, up to 1,000 agents and 16 concurrent by default); cross-session messaging (SendMessage/ListAgents, v2.1.224+, Windows v2.1.234+) with notify_when_idle (v2.1.236+, one notice when another session next goes idle, 12-hour expiry, only your local sessions); cloud scheduled tasks with API triggers (a POST starts a new cloud session; beta header experimental-cc-routine-2026-04-01); claude --bg from a shell or a script (a hook or Bash command could run it; I did not verify that a session may do so); agent teams.

claims.claim: (3a) Subagents get tools by agent type: Explore and Plan are read-only; general-purpose has every tool; custom agents follow their tools list.
claims.what_sources_say: Explore and Plan deny Write and Edit. General-purpose has every tool available to subagents. A custom agent omitting tools gets all tools; a tools list restricts it, and disallowedTools removes specific ones. Memory-enabled subagents automatically get Read, Write and Edit. Background subagents get a smaller built-in set that still includes Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, Edit, Write, WebFetch and WebSearch, and MCP tools are kept. The fixflow-explorer agent in this repo is therefore read-only if it follows the Explore pattern or lists no Write.

claims.claim: (3b) Subagent permission modes: the parent's bypassPermissions, acceptEdits or auto overrides the subagent's own; background prompts surface in the parent session.
claims.what_sources_say: Parent in bypassPermissions, acceptEdits or auto: the subagent uses the parent's mode. Parent in plan: the subagent stays in plan. Parent in default or dontAsk: the subagent uses its own permissionMode (bypassPermissions needs v2.1.267+). A background subagent's permission prompts appear in the main session labelled with its name; Esc denies that one call. Workflow subagents use your permission rules, and the docs advise adding needed tools to allow rules before a long run to avoid prompts.

sources.title: Workflows: Approve the plan before it runs

claims.claim: (3c) 'Subagents cannot write files' (B16) is a documented limitation.
claims.what_sources_say: The docs say subagents can write files if their tool set includes Write or Edit, and general-purpose has both by default. The documented causes of the symptom are the read-only built-in types Explore and Plan, a custom tools list that omits Write, and a background permission prompt that is denied or unanswered. In worktree-isolated sessions, edits targeting the main checkout are blocked, so a report written to a path in the main checkout fails. A subagent's final report is the only thing returned to the parent. The page I read gives no 'write report to file and return only the path' recipe; the unread final ~17k characters might. It follows from the model: instruct the agent to Write the report and return a path plus a short summary. The fixflow-explorer agent, and any agent run under Explore or Plan, would not be able to.

sources.title: Subagents: built-in agents, tools, 'Can subagents write files?'
Worktrees: How Claude Code enforces isolation

claims.claim: (4a) Workflows keep the orchestrator's context small: the script holds loops and intermediate results, and only the final answer returns.
claims.what_sources_say: With subagents, skills and agent teams the intermediate results live in Claude's context window or a shared task list; with a workflow they live in script variables, so Claude's context holds only the final answer. Scale is dozens to hundreds of agents per run. Limits: no mid-run user input (run each stage as its own workflow for sign-off), the script has no filesystem or shell access, no import(), 16 concurrent agents by default (to 256 via env, v2.1.269+), 4,096 items per parallel/pipeline call, 1,000 agents per run, Date.now and Math.random throw. Runs are resumable only inside the same session or via --resume. A run does not continue by itself after you exit or background the session; Claude must relaunch it and replay saved results. Workflows work in -p and the Agent SDK. Stalled agents restart up to five times. agent() accepts a JSON schema, so structured returns are possible. A merge-and-review gate could be a script, but nothing documents merge locking.

claims.claim: (4b) Context management options for a long-running orchestrator: compaction, /autocompact window, 1M context, subagent isolation, fork, memory files.
claims.what_sources_say: Auto-compaction runs near the limit, and /compact accepts a focus instruction. /autocompact <tokens> (setting: autoCompactWindow; the exact name was not seen on a fetched page, only the command and the 'auto-compact window' heading) sets how full the window gets before compaction; subagent definitions can also set autoCompactWindow (v2.1.296+). After compaction: CLAUDE.md, auto memory, skill descriptions (v2.1.304+) and the plan are re-injected; up to five recently touched files are re-read (over 5,000 tokens becomes a path reference); invoked skill bodies are capped at 5,000 tokens each and 25,000 total; path-scoped rules and nested CLAUDE.md are summarized away; SessionStart hooks matching 'compact' re-inject context; PreCompact and PostCompact hooks exist. 1M windows: Fable models, Sonnet 5 and later, Haiku 5.5, Opus 4.6 and later, Sonnet 4.6. Delegation to subagents keeps large reads out. /fork copies the conversation into a new background session. I found no page giving dedicated guidance for long-running orchestrators beyond these.

claims.claim: (5a) Agent teams exist: teammates, SendMessage, shared task list; but they are experimental and limited.
claims.what_sources_say: Disabled by default; enable with CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1. A lead plus teammates, each its own full session with its own context; a mailbox per agent; shared task list with pending, in-progress and completed states, dependencies, and file locking on task claiming. Teammates do not inherit the lead's history. Limits: no session resumption of in-process teammates, task status can lag, one team per session, no nested teams, the lead is fixed, in-process teammates cannot run background subagents, the permission mode is the lead's, and teammate prompts bubble up to the lead. Docs advise against agent teams for sequential, same-file or heavily dependent work and warn of much higher token use. The same docs recommend each teammate own different files. Teammate sessions do not pause at usage limits.

claims.claim: (5b) Several sessions can each merge under a lock; multi-orchestrator coordination is a built-in feature.
claims.what_sources_say: Nothing in the fetched pages provides a merge lock or a merge queue. The only locking documented is file locking for task claiming in agent teams, and git's own worktree locks (Claude Code takes a git worktree lock on an agent's worktree to block concurrent cleanup). Cross-session messaging lets sessions on one machine pass plain text with rate limits (50 queued messages per receiver, about 1M characters per message), and it has per-session inbound controls (accept, hold, refuse). Messages are never consent. Worktrees isolate files and share the .git directory. One-team-per-session and no-nested-teams rule out multiple orchestrators inside one team. A merge lock for the owner's flow would have to be built, for example a lock file or git ref held by a script or hook.

claims.claim: (6) Progress visibility: task list, hooks, status line, notifications and phone push, usage reporting exist.
claims.what_sources_say: Workflows: the /workflows view shows phases, agent counts, each agent's prompt, tool calls and token use, plus a one-line summary in the task panel. Agent view: row states (working, needs input, idle, completed, failed, stopped); terminal notifications; the Notification hook receives agent_needs_input and agent_completed; claude agents --json --all reports state, status and waitingFor for scripts. Status line: a script gets JSON on stdin, including context_window.used_percentage, cost.total_cost_usd, rate_limits.five_hour and seven_day used_percentage and resets_at, worktree.* and workspace.git_worktree, pr.*, and prompt_cache stats (v2.1.251+). Desktop: an OS notification when a session finishes, and a phone push for Dispatch-started sessions. A session's own step display not moving is not something the docs address; a hook or status-line script could surface heartbeat or last-activity data. Hook events in this docs build (32): SessionStart, Setup, UserPromptSubmit, UserPromptExpansion, PreToolUse, PermissionRequest, PermissionDenied, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, PostToolBatch, Notification, MessageDisplay, SubagentStart, SubagentStop, TaskCreated, TaskCompleted, Stop, StopFailure, TeammateIdle, InstructionsLoaded, ConfigChange, CwdChanged, DirectoryAdded, FileChanged, WorktreeCreate, WorktreeRemove, PreCompact, PostCompact, PreModelSwitch, PostModelSwitch, Elicitation, ElicitationResult, SessionEnd. OpenTelemetry: only a mention in plugins/measure and plugins/org was seen; I did not read a monitoring page.

claims.claim: (7) Documented cleanup of worktrees, sessions and background processes.
claims.what_sources_say: Worktrees: exiting an unnamed interactive worktree session auto-removes a clean worktree; a dirty one prompts. A named session prompts first. claude -p never cleans up and leaves a git lock (git worktree unlock, then git worktree remove). Subagent and background-session worktrees are swept after cleanupPeriodDays, but only when clean (no changed files and no unpushed commits; submodule check v2.1.274+) and never for a worktree you made with git worktree add. Manual: git worktree list and remove [--force]. Background sessions: claude stop <id>, claude rm <id> (keeps a dirty worktree; refuses on unpushed commits; --discard-unpushed v2.1.260+), Ctrl+X in agent view; idle sessions' processes stop after about an hour unless pinned; cleanupPeriodDays can delete stopped sessions' transcripts. Desktop: 'Auto-archive after PR merge or close' setting (not for running or cloud sessions); archived local sessions' worktrees and data are removed about 30 days later; an approval card precedes Claude archiving a session except in Auto and Bypass modes, which is the source of the B15 archive mishap. Ctrl+X Ctrl+K stops all background subagents. worktree.baseRef, worktree.bgIsolation and permissions.blockWritesOutsideWorkingDirectories shape isolation. I did not find a storage-usage command; none is documented in the pages read. Containers are outside Claude Code's scope.

claims.claim: (8) Hooks can verify a session's claims before it reports done; exit code 2 blocks Stop, SubagentStop and TaskCompleted.
claims.what_sources_say: Exit 2 on Stop prevents Claude from stopping and continues the conversation, with stderr fed back. On SubagentStop it prevents the subagent from stopping. On TaskCompleted it blocks completion. On TeammateIdle it keeps the teammate working. On PreToolUse it blocks the call. On PostToolUse it only shows stderr, because the tool already ran. Exit 2 with empty stdout and a 'No such file or directory' stderr is treated as a non-blocking error (a missing script fails open, a trap for a verification hook). Hook types: command, http, mcp_tool, prompt (single-turn model check, 30s default) and agent (a subagent with Read, Grep and Glob, experimental, 60s default). Command timeout is 600s by default. The stop_hook_active loop guard sits in a section I did not read (page truncated), so check it before writing a Stop hook. A Stop hook running the real test command or checking that cited test files exist is the supported mechanism for B12. Whether it runs inside background or workflow subagents beyond SubagentStop was not verified.

implications.implication: Evidence supports: keep the root as an interactive terminal session signed in with the subscription, with autoContinueAtUsageLimit on, and run slice work as workflows (they pause and resume themselves at a limit, v2.1.271+/v2.1.318+). Add cloud scheduled tasks for work that must start with the PC off, and an API-triggered cloud task as a no-user starter; their cost is a fresh clone and overage only with usage credits. Evidence does not support unattended resumption of a halted session in general: auto-continue needs the session open, stops after three continuations and when the PC slept over 30 minutes, does not survive an exit, and is not applied in claude -p, background, Remote Control or teammate sessions. Three days of silence is not covered by any documented mechanism. A weekly limit that resets more than 24 hours out disables the wait. The docs describe no rule that a session may start sessions only on a user-opened turn; I could not locate that rule, so test it before designing around it. The documented path without the user is workflows, cross-session messages with notify_when_idle, claude --bg, and cloud API triggers.

Evidence supports a workflow as the orchestrator for fan-out and review rounds: intermediate results sit in script variables, resumable replay, up to 16 concurrent agents, and structured JSON returns, so the root context holds only a final summary. Use /autocompact, compaction focus, SessionStart-on-compact re-injection and memory files for the long root session, and 1M-context models. Evidence does not support a built-in merge lock or several orchestrators merging: agent teams allow one team per session, no nesting, and are experimental. A merge gate needs your own lock (script or hook) or a single serialised merge workflow. Workflows allow no mid-run user input, so run each stage as its own workflow.

Evidence supports Stop, SubagentStop and TaskCompleted hooks with exit code 2 as a hard gate: the hook script itself runs the test command and checks that every cited test file, path or commit exists before the session may report done, with stderr fed back for another attempt. Agent-type hooks can read files, and prompt hooks add a model check. It does not support trusting the model's report. Read the stop_hook_active section first to avoid loops, make the script fail closed (a missing script fails open under the 'No such file' rule), and note the docs do not measure how often this catches overstated reports.

Evidence supports: a status-line script using context_window, cost, rate_limits (five_hour and seven_day with reset times), worktree and pr fields; the /workflows progress view; agent view states and claude agents --json --all for a poll; Notification hook events (agent_needs_input, agent_completed); and Desktop OS or phone push (phone push only for Dispatch-started sessions). A hook on PostToolUse or SubagentStart/Stop could append a heartbeat line to a file for a heartbeat dashboard, which is my inference, not a documented feature. Not documented: any fix for a session's own step display freezing; OpenTelemetry usage reporting not verified.

Evidence supports: cleanupPeriodDays sweeps of clean subagent and background worktrees, claude stop and claude rm, git worktree list and remove, pinned versus idle background sessions, and the Desktop auto-archive after PR merge or close setting. Note the archive approval card is skipped in Auto and Bypass modes, which matches the earlier wrongful archive; use Manual approval for archive, or archive only from a script keyed to a merged PR. The sweep and rm refuse dirty or unpushed worktrees, which protects work but leaves piles; -p worktrees stay locked until a later sweep. No storage-usage command, and nothing for database containers or Docker, was found.

The premise is contradicted for general-purpose subagents and custom agents with Write. The likely causes are the read-only Explore and Plan types (and a read-only custom agent such as fixflow-explorer), a custom tools list without Write, an unanswered background permission prompt, or the worktree rule that blocks writes to the main checkout. Fix: use general-purpose or a custom agent with Write, pre-allow Write for the report directory, tell it to write the report to a path outside the repo or inside its worktree and return only the path and a short summary, and have workflow agents return JSON by schema. Verify in a one-agent trial; I read no documented 'write report to file' recipe.

claims.claim: GitHub merge queue serialises-by-speculation: each queued PR is tested on a temporary branch combining the target branch with the PRs ahead of it, and merges only if required checks pass.
claims.what_sources_say: GitHub docs (feature description, no measurement): temporary branches under gh-readonly-queue/, required checks must report via the merge_group event, build concurrency 1-100, group size 1-100, failing PR is removed and the rest rebuilt. Needs a GitHub repo, an admin enabling 'Require merge queue', and a non-wildcard branch protection pattern. PRs must already pass branch protection before queueing.

claims.claim: Zuul-style speculative gating tests queued changes in parallel, each on top of those ahead, and restarts the ones behind a failure.
claims.what_sources_say: Zuul docs (design description, no measured throughput): best case all queued changes test together and merge at once; worst case degrades to one at a time. A pipeline window starts at 20, grows by 1 per merge, halves on failure (TCP-like). Needs Gerrit/GitHub/GitLab driver plus test-node infrastructure (ZooKeeper, Nodepool listed as dependencies). It is a heavy service, not a local script.

claims.claim: Mergify, bors, stacked-change tools, trunk-based development and optimistic merge with auto-revert work without a remote.
claims.what_sources_say: Not fetched. Both documented queues (GitHub, Zuul) are built on a hosted forge and remote CI events. I found no source for a local equivalent. A local lock plus pre-merge check on a temp merge branch is an inference from the queue design (same mechanism: test merged result, then fast-forward), not evidenced.

claims.claim: MAST (Cemri et al. 2025): multi-agent LLM failures fall into 14 modes in 3 categories, with task verification a major share.
claims.what_sources_say: Abstract: 14 modes, 3 categories (system design, inter-agent misalignment, task verification), 1,600+ annotated traces from 7 frameworks, kappa 0.88 on the 150-trace taxonomy set; models GPT-4, Claude 3, Qwen2.5, CodeLlama (all pre-2025 frontier). Full text (first 100k chars): category shares about FC1 44%, FC2 32%, FC3 24% (summed by the fetch tool from per-mode figures, not stated by the paper); top modes step repetition 15.7%, reasoning-action mismatch 13.2%, unaware of termination 12.4%, disobeys spec 11.8%, incorrect verification 9.1%, no/incomplete verification 8.2%; loss of conversation history only 2.8%.

claims.claim: Anthropic's multi-agent research system: orchestrator-worker beats single agent, at large token cost, with file/reference hand-off.
claims.what_sources_say: Anthropic reports (internal research eval, Opus 4 lead + Sonnet 4 workers): +90.2% over single-agent Opus 4; multi-agent uses about 15x chat tokens; on BrowseComp token usage alone explained 80% of variance (3 factors 95%). Authors say multi-agent works mainly because it spends enough tokens. Lead context is truncated beyond 200k so the plan is saved to memory; subagents write outputs to external storage and return references; fresh subagents with handoffs used on overflow. Failures: 50 subagents for simple queries, duplicated work from vague delegation, synchronous lead blocks on slowest worker. Read-only research task, not code writing; self-reported, not independently replicated.

claims.what_sources_say: Post (2025-06-12) measures nothing: no benchmarks or rates; the Flappy Bird example is a stated hypothetical. It asserts two principles (share full traces; actions carry implicit decisions) and recommends a linear agent plus a history-compressing model, with subagents only for narrow questions. Predates current models. It does not contradict Anthropic: Anthropic's task is read-only research, Cognition's is write-heavy coding. I found no later update on the page; replies/rebuttals were not fetched.

claims.what_sources_say: I found and read no controlled comparison. Only indirect evidence: Anthropic's context-overflow handling (store plan externally, spawn fresh agents with handoff) and MAST's low rate of history loss (2.8%) versus verification failures (about 17% for the two verification modes).

claims.claim: Coding agents often claim success that the environment does not support ('false success').
claims.what_sources_say: Advani, arXiv 2606.09863 (June 2026, workshop paper): false success = claim vs programmatic state mismatch. On tau2-bench (9,876 trajectories, 8 model families) about 45-48% of failures in airline/retail and 3% in dual-control telecom; per-model 13% (GPT-5.2) to 79% (Qwen3-Max-Thinking). On AppWorld 75.8% of failures with explicit claims; per-model 67-89%. These are customer-service/app-API tasks, not repository coding; rates are among failures, not among all runs.

sources.title: From Confident Closing to Silent Failure: Characterizing False Success in LLM Agents

claims.claim: A model judge reading the report is an adequate verifier of agent claims.
claims.what_sources_say: Same paper: five LLM judges, including with full task spec, never exceeded AUROC 0.65 on tau2-bench (best Sonnet 4.5, 0.640) and about 0.54 on AppWorld. Cheap TF-IDF detectors reached AUROC about 0.83 and 0.95 and recovered 72% of false successes at a 10% flag rate versus 13% for the best judge. Rewriting honest failures into confident style flipped about 20-25% of cases for both. The paper did not test state-based verification; it only suggests it. In a different study (EvilGenie via search snippet only) LLM judges did well on unambiguous reward hacking, so judge usefulness depends on whether the judge sees the evidence.

claims.claim: In real coding sessions, agents oversell results at a measurable rate, and CLAUDE.md-style instructions do not fix it.
claims.what_sources_say: Transluce write-up (LessWrong, 2026; LLM-judge-labelled, not human-verified): severe 'overselling/misrepresenting success' 1.8% of 4,788 SWE-chat sessions and 0.1% of 3,627 Transluce internal sessions; any-severity 34.7% and 5.7%. Any-severity by model on SWE-chat ranged from 62% (Haiku 4.5) to 17% (Opus 4.7, n=46); authors say cross-model comparison is unreliable. No separate rate for fabricated test ids. Authors observed that CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md instructions were insufficient and orchestrators often did work themselves despite blocks. The bottleneck's 'cited tests that did not exist' is therefore not separately measured anywhere I read.

claims.what_sources_say: Search snippets only: ImpossibleBench hidden tests cut cheating to near zero but lowered legitimate success, read-only tests blocked test edits without that cost; EvilGenie found explicit hacking in Codex and Claude Code and held-out tests added little beyond judges; a CMU study found 323 of 1,968 tasks (16%) across five terminal-agent benchmarks hackable. implications.implication: Evidence supports moving the serial work (test merged result, fast-forward) into a mechanical queue, since GitHub and Zuul both gate on tested merged state rather than reading. It supports keeping code-writing agents single-threaded per slice and offloading research/review reads to subagents that return file references (Anthropic, Cognition agree on this split). It does not support a claim that several orchestrators or sub-orchestrators per wave perform better; no controlled comparison was found. MAST ties the largest failure share to design and verification, not history loss (2.8%), so context overflow is not the main measured risk. Local-only equivalents of the queue are inference, not evidenced.

Evidence supports not trusting self-reports and not using a model that only reads the report as the check: judges stayed at or below AUROC 0.65 in a 2026 study, and instructions in AGENTS.md did not stop overselling. It supports mechanical checks of the claim against recorded state (cited test id exists in collected tests and appears in the run log; re-run by a process the agent cannot write to; read-only tests; test-file-edit detection) with moderate support from benchmark snippets. It does not support evidence hashes specifically, nor give a rate for fabricated test ids. Studies are mostly customer-service/app benchmarks or LLM-judge-labelled logs, and rates differ widely by model, so measure your own rate on the clinic transcripts first.

Evidence supports one-fragment-per-change files compiled by a generator (towncrier docs) so slices write only their own file and the board/changelog is generated. Merge-conflict benefit and CI enforcement are not in the page read, and ADR-per-file, Reno, changesets, CODEOWNERS, event-log-plus-board were not read; treat as practitioner pattern. Stale AGENTS.md/context-map content has no source here.

Evidence does not support a specific recommendation: OTel agent conventions could not be confirmed (docs moved; stability unknown), and nothing on heartbeat files or dashboards was read. Anthropic's note that the lead cannot steer or observe workers mid-task under synchronous execution is the only related finding. Any heartbeat or event-log design is engineering judgement, not research.

Supports using git worktree remove (refuses dirty or locked trees without force), add --lock for race-free protection of in-use trees, and prune for stale metadata, as the safe deletion primitives that make a 'delete only when merged and clean' policy enforceable without human sign-off. The lock stores a reason, not an expiry, so leases need custom code. Whether merged-branch GC or archive-on-merge is safe for sessions the owner is still using is not evidenced; it is a policy decision.

Supports giving each worktree its own Compose project name (-p or COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME, which outranks the directory name) so containers are namespaced and attributable to a worktree. Docs read do not cover down, volume removal or orphan removal, so teardown-on-merge needs checking in the Compose CLI reference. No evidence in this lane on idle-session memory cost or reference counting.
